blocks.body: Over five days in May 2020, 7.35 inches of rain fell on Skokie, with 3.41 inches on May 17 alone. The regional deep tunnel system reached capacity, and many basements backed up. The village's flood control program holds water in the streets for up to four hours after rain stops, which protects many homes, but not every basement. The village has encouraged backflow valves or overhead sewers for homes with repeat backups.

blocks.h2: Sewer Backup Questions From Skokie Homeowners

items.q: Why does my floor drain back up in big storms?
items.preview: Either your line is blocked or the sewer is full.
items.answer: Either your line is partly blocked, or the sewer system is full and pushing back. We clear and camera your line to tell which.

items.q: Can I prevent storm backups without an overhead sewer?
items.preview: A backflow valve may be enough.
items.answer: Sometimes. A backflow valve on the main line can stop sewer water from flowing back in. For basements with fixtures, an overhead sewer is more complete.

items.q: Is a sewer backup covered by insurance?
items.answer: Many policies need a sewer backup rider. Check with your agent.

items.q: What should I throw away after a backup?
items.preview: Porous items that soaked up sewage.
items.answer: Porous items like carpet, padding and cardboard that soaked up sewage usually can't be saved. A restoration company can advise on the rest.

items.q: Why was there water in the street after the 2020 storm?
items.answer: Skokie's flood control program holds water on streets for a few hours to keep it out of basements.

items.q: How much does sewer backup service cost in Skokie?
items.preview: It depends on the cause. You'll approve a flat price first.
items.answer: It depends on what caused it and how we reach the line. You'll approve a flat-rate price before we start.
